result:
**Read it if you're building a SKILL.md linter or rubric; skip it if you want evidence that these smells cause harm.**

The paper is the first empirical study of SKILL.md files as artifacts. Three deliverables: a component taxonomy (13 higher / 44 lower-level), 26 "skill smells" derived by inverting community best practices, and an automated detector.

**What's directly usable**

The 26-smell catalog is a ready rubric skeleton, split cleanly into 5 static checks (word/char caps on body/name/description, backslash paths, XML-in-frontmatter) and 21 LLM-judge checks. Their judge framing is copyable: per-smell definition, one positive and one negative example, binary answer, thinking mode. Detector scores weighted F1 0.78 / precision 0.79 / recall 0.78 on 53 hand-labeled files.

**Headline findings**

Over 99% of 238 marketplace skills carry at least one smell, averaging 10.5 each; only one file is clean. Rationalization Loophole (nothing discourages skipping required steps) hits 94%. Component use is thin past the basics: Task 74%, Introduction 64%, References 57%, then a steep drop to under 5% for most of the taxonomy. Six of 13 higher-level components have no community guidance at all. Smells rarely get removed once introduced.

**Why the results are weak**

The best practices are folklore: 29 web sources, majority-voted on conflicts, never causally validated. So the paper shows smells are common, not that they hurt. The sample is popular public marketplace skills only, and the detector numbers rest on 53 labeled files judged by a single 4-bit quantized open model.

**Bottom-line read**: skim the smell catalog and the judge prompt design, take the F1 0.78 as a baseline to beat, and treat every prevalence number as descriptive.
